title: Shot dead by police: funeral of former hockey player Brandon Christian in Beauce
subtitle: The funeral of former hockey player Brandon Christian, who was shot dead by police earlier this month, was held in Beauce.
article: The funeral of former hockey player Brandon Christian, who was shot dead by police earlier this month, was held Saturday in Saint-Georges, in Beauce.

On February 2, Brandon Christian's wife, Sonia Drouin, called the Sûreté du Québec because the 47-year-old man was in crisis. The officers dispatched to the scene tried to subdue him with a conducted energy weapon and pepper spray, but it didn't work.
An officer eventually opened fire on the former hockey player, who was transported to a hospital where his death was confirmed.
The family continues to denounce the police intervention that led to the death of Brandon Christian, who had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.
"They didn't want me to be part of the intervention plan," said Sonia Drouin, who had been married to Brandon Christian for 15 years.

"This wasn't an intervention like usual. Usually, they come, it takes six days. This time they showed up and fired eight bullets into his body. I don't call that subduing someone, I call that shooting someone down, and it won't stay like this. I hope he will be the last person with mental health problems to be shot down like a dog," continued the widow.
His brother-in-law, Jean-Pierre Drouin, also insists the police knew about the man's health issues.

"This wasn't the first time they intervened, and it had always gone well. I don't understand why this time it turned out this way. It's illogical. He wasn't someone aggressive," said Jean-Pierre Drouin on Saturday, on the sidelines of the funeral held at the Centre Évangélique Renaissance in Saint-Georges.
According to him, the police should have given Brandon Christian space, let him go, and he would have eventually returned home.
"We were afraid of finding him frozen to death in a snowbank, but it ended with them shooting him down," added Mr. Drouin.
He said that when his sister called the police, it was to get help for her husband, originally from Burlington, Ontario. She wasn't afraid of him.
"There was a lack of communication because what happened makes no sense. They shot him eight times," he said.
The family hopes to get answers once the investigation by the Bureau of Independent Investigations (BEI) is completed.
"What happened? What was said? We want things to change," concluded the deceased's brother-in-law.
